title: Marriage, Celibacy, Children, and the Rich Young Man
summary: Leaving Galilee for the last time, Jesus is tested by Pharisees on whether a man may divorce his wife for any reason, and he answers from God's design at creation, allowing an exception for sexual immorality and adding that some renounce marriage for the sake of the kingdom. He blesses little children, and he tells a rich young man who has kept the commandments to sell his possessions and follow him, which the man cannot do. Jesus warns how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom, says that with God all things are possible, and promises the Twelve thrones in the renewal of all things and everyone who has left all for his sake a hundredfold and eternal life.
story:
Chapter 19 opens the last great stage of Matthew's story. The formula “When Jesus had finished saying these things” closes the fourth discourse, the teaching on the community in chapter 18, as similar sentences close each of the five discourses (7:28, 11:1, 13:53, 26:1). Jesus now leaves Galilee and does not return until after the resurrection (28:16). From here to the end of chapter 20 he is on the road south toward Jerusalem, where he has three times said he will suffer, die, and rise (16:21, 17:22-23, 20:17-19), and he teaches his disciples as they walk.

The topics are the ordinary structures of a household: husband and wife, children, property and inheritance. Matthew follows Mark 10:1-31 closely but adds material of his own: the disciples' dismay and the saying about eunuchs (verses 10 to 12), the promise of twelve thrones (verse 28), and, straight after the chapter, the parable of the vineyard workers (20:1-16), which the saying about the first and the last frames on both sides (19:30, 20:16). In each unit Jesus overturns an accepted order. Marriage is not a contract a husband may end at will but a union God has made. Children, who had no standing, show how the kingdom is received. Wealth, widely taken as a sign of God's favor, can bar the way to it. Chapter 18 had taught the disciples to become like children and to forgive without limit; chapter 19 presses the same humility into marriage, money, and ambition, and it ends with Peter's question, what will we receive, which the next chapter answers with a story about grace.
historical:
‘The region of Judea beyond the Jordan’ (verse 1) is Perea, the strip east of the river that belonged, with Galilee, to Herod Antipas, tetrarch from 4 BC to AD 39. Josephus says Antipas held John the Baptist at his Perean fortress of Machaerus and put him to death there (Antiquities 18.116-119), and Matthew has already told how John died for condemning Antipas's marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife (14:3-4). Josephus adds that Herodias had divorced her living husband to marry Antipas, which he calls a flouting of ancestral law (Antiquities 18.136). A question about divorce asked in Antipas's territory, of a prophet whom many linked with John, was not academic.

The Pharisees' question in verse 3 is worded as only Matthew words it: whether a man may divorce his wife ‘for any reason’ (kata pasan aitian). That phrase names one side of a live debate over Deuteronomy 24:1, which allowed a man to divorce his wife if he found in her ‘some indecency’ (Hebrew ervat davar). The Mishnah records how the schools of two first-century teachers read the words (m. Gittin 9:10): the house of Shammai stressed ‘indecency’ and allowed divorce only for sexual unfaithfulness, while the house of Hillel stressed ‘some thing’ and allowed it even if she spoiled his cooking; Rabbi Akiva, a generation after Jesus, added even if the husband found a woman more beautiful. The Hillelite view was the common practice. Josephus paraphrases the law as permitting a man to divorce his wife for any cause whatever (Antiquities 4.253), Philo speaks of a woman divorced on any pretext (Special Laws 3.30), and Josephus himself divorced his wife because he was displeased with her conduct (Life 426). Some Jewish groups were far stricter. The Damascus Document from the Dead Sea community cites ‘male and female he created them’ (Genesis 1:27), the text Jesus quotes in verse 4, against taking a second wife in a man's lifetime (CD 4:20-21), and the Temple Scroll forbids the king to take another wife while the first lives (11QTemple 57:17-19). The question therefore invites Jesus to take the Hillelite side or the Shammaite side. He answers from creation, and his exception in verse 9 is close in wording to the Shammaite position, while his refusal of the husband's second marriage goes beyond both schools.

Jewish and Roman law differed. Under Roman law either spouse could end a marriage, and divorce was common in the upper classes. In Jewish law only the husband could issue a divorce: the Mishnah states that a woman may be divorced with or without her consent, but a man only by his own will (m. Yevamot 14:1). A woman in an intolerable marriage could ask a court to compel her husband to divorce her in certain cases, but she could not divorce him herself. That imbalance is the setting for Jesus' words, which bind the one who held the power.

Eunuchs were a familiar presence in the courts of the ancient Near East and the Roman world, often as chamberlains and treasurers, like the Ethiopian official in Acts 8:27. Deuteronomy 23:1 excluded a man with crushed or cut genitals from the assembly of the LORD, yet Isaiah 56:3-5 promised faithful eunuchs a place in God's house and a name better than sons and daughters, and Wisdom 3:14 calls blessed the eunuch whose hands have done no wrong. The rabbis distinguished a ‘eunuch of the sun’ (saris hammah), born so, from a ‘eunuch of man’ (saris adam), made so by others (m. Yevamot 8:4), which matches the first two of Jesus' three kinds. His third kind, those who ‘live like eunuchs’ (literally ‘made themselves eunuchs’) for the kingdom, had few parallels in Jewish life, where marriage and children were a duty; Josephus says some Essenes refrained from marriage (Jewish War 2.120-121), and Philo describes the celibate Therapeutae near Alexandria (On the Contemplative Life 68). Justin Martyr, writing in Rome about AD 155, reports that a young Christian in Alexandria petitioned the governor Felix for permission to have a surgeon castrate him and was refused (First Apology 29), which shows that the saying could be taken literally and that the church did not require it.

The promise of twelve thrones (verse 28) draws on Jewish hope for the restoration of the twelve tribes. Daniel 7:9 sees thrones set in place for judgment, and the Psalms of Solomon, written in the first century BC, pray for a son of David who will gather a holy people and judge the tribes of the people (Psalms of Solomon 17:26). By Jesus' day ten of the tribes had been scattered since the Assyrian conquest of 722 BC, so a promise that the Twelve would judge the twelve tribes announced the regathering of all Israel.
cultural:
Marriage in first-century Judaism was arranged between families, often when the bride was in her early teens, and it was a legal and economic contract as much as a personal bond. The husband's divorce was a private act that needed no court. He had a bill of divorce (the get) written and handed to his wife, and its essential words, as the Mishnah gives them, were ‘behold, you are permitted to any man’ (m. Gittin 9:3): the document protected the woman by proving she was free to remarry. She received the sum pledged in her marriage contract (the ketubbah), which was meant to discourage hasty divorce, and she usually returned to her father's house or had to find a new husband to survive. That is why Jesus holds the husband responsible for what follows. The Babylonian Talmud closes its tractate on divorce with Rabbi Eleazar's saying that the altar itself sheds tears over a man who divorces the wife of his youth (b. Gittin 90b, drawing on Malachi 2:13-16); Jewish tradition grieved divorce even as it regulated it.

Adultery in Jewish law was defined by the woman's marital status. A man who slept with another man's wife committed adultery against her husband; a married man who slept with an unmarried woman did not commit adultery in the legal sense, and a man might lawfully have more than one wife. When Jesus says that a man who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery (verse 9), he treats the husband's second marriage as a breach of the first, which placed husband and wife under one standard.

The Greek eunouchos stands in the Greek Old Testament for the Hebrew saris, which could mean a castrated man or simply a court official; Potiphar, who had a wife, is called Pharaoh's saris (Genesis 39:1). Jesus' first two kinds are literal: men born incapable of marriage and men castrated by others, usually as slaves. The third kind is figurative, as the disciples' remark about not marrying shows: those who forgo marriage and children, the ordinary hope of every Jewish man, for the sake of the kingdom. Jesus himself was unmarried, as were John the Baptist and, at least in his mission years, Paul (1 Corinthians 7:7-8).

Parents brought children to respected teachers and elders for a blessing, and Matthew alone says they wanted Jesus to lay his hands on them and pray (verse 13), the gesture of Jacob blessing Joseph's sons (Genesis 48:14). Jewish families still bless their sons on the eve of the Sabbath with the words of Genesis 48:20. Children had no legal standing and could offer nothing in return, so the disciples treated them as an interruption.

Wealth was widely taken as a mark of God's favor, since Deuteronomy promised prosperity to the obedient (Deuteronomy 28:1-14), though the prophets condemned riches gained by oppression. The young man's ‘great wealth’ (verse 22, ktēmata) probably means estates in land, the most secure form of wealth and the basis of a family's standing. ‘Treasure in heaven’ was a Jewish expression for reward stored up with God through mercy to the poor (Tobit 4:8-9, Sirach 29:11-12). The camel was the largest animal commonly seen in the land and the eye of a needle the smallest opening in daily use, so verse 24 is a deliberate impossibility. The Babylonian Talmud uses an elephant passing through the eye of a needle in the same way: as something too absurd to appear even in a dream (b. Berakhot 55b), and as a jibe at scholars who could make an absurd argument sound plausible (b. Bava Metzia 38b). Two later explanations soften the saying and have no ancient support. Cyril of Alexandria, in the fifth century, proposed that ‘camel’ (kamēlos) should be read as kamilos, a ship's cable; the idea of a small gate in Jerusalem's wall called the needle's eye first appears in a medieval gloss attributed to Anselm, which Thomas Aquinas collected in his Catena Aurea. No such gate is known from any ancient source, and both explanations miss that Jesus is describing what only God can do (verse 26).

The ‘hundredfold’ of verse 29 echoes the harvest language of the parable of the sower (13:8, 23), and ‘inherit eternal life’ uses the language of Israel inheriting the land as God's gift (Deuteronomy 4:1) to speak of the life of the age to come.
literary:
The chapter has three units, each set off by someone coming to Jesus: the Pharisees on divorce (verses 3 to 12), the children brought for blessing (13 to 15), and the young man, followed by the discussion with the disciples (16 to 30). The divorce debate follows the form of a controversy story: a testing question, an answer from Scripture, a counter-question from the law, a ruling, and a private word to the disciples. Matthew arranges Mark's material more tightly. In Mark, Jesus asks what Moses commanded and the Pharisees answer with what he permitted; in Matthew, Jesus goes straight to creation, joining Genesis 1:27 and 2:24, and the Pharisees object that Moses ‘ordered’ a certificate, to which Jesus replies that Moses ‘permitted’ divorce. The contrast between command and concession carries the argument, and the phrase ‘from the beginning’ frames Jesus' answer (verses 4 and 8).

Matthew's additions change the shape of the teaching. The exception clause (verse 9) matches the one in the Sermon on the Mount (5:32). The disciples' dismay (verse 10) and Jesus' reply about eunuchs (verses 11 and 12), found only here, turn from marriage to its renunciation, and the saying is framed by two statements about receiving: ‘not everyone can accept this word’ and ‘the one who can accept this should accept it’. Scholars disagree whether ‘this word’ in verse 11 points back to Jesus' teaching on divorce or to the disciples' remark that it is better not to marry; the answer affects how the eunuch saying is read.

The young man's story turns on the word good. In Mark and Luke he calls Jesus ‘Good Teacher’ and Jesus asks why he calls him good; in Matthew he asks what good thing he must do, and Jesus asks why he asks about what is good, adding that there is only One who is good (verses 16 and 17). Matthew alone calls him young (verses 20 and 22), Luke alone a ruler (Luke 18:18); all three say he was rich. Jesus lists commandments from the second table of the Ten Commandments, and Matthew alone adds ‘love your neighbor as yourself’ from Leviticus 19:18, the command he treats as a summary of the law (22:39-40). The man's question, ‘What do I still lack?’ is answered with ‘if you want to be perfect’ (teleios), the word of 5:48, and the command to follow. Matthew omits Mark's note that Jesus looked at him and loved him (Mark 10:21), and he omits Mark's ‘in this present age, along with persecutions’ from the promise of verse 29.

The last unit moves from impossibility to promise. The disciples' question, ‘Who then can be saved?’ receives Jesus' answer that with God all things are possible, an echo of the angel's word to Sarah (Genesis 18:14). Peter's question, ‘What then will there be for us?’ receives the promise of thrones and the hundredfold, but the chapter ends with a warning that many first will be last, a saying repeated in reverse at 20:16 to frame the parable that follows.

outline.t: Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea beyond the Jordan
Marriage and those who forgo it for the kingdom
Riches and the kingdom: impossible with man
The reward of those who follow

doctrines.note: Jesus grounds marriage in creation, joining Genesis 1:27 and 2:24: God made them male and female, the two become one flesh, and what God has joined no human should separate. Moses' provision for divorce regulated hard hearts rather than expressing God's design. Matthew records an exception for sexual immorality (verse 9), whose meaning the traditions read differently, and he sets beside marriage an honored calling to forgo it for the kingdom (verse 12) and a welcome for children as those to whom the kingdom belongs.

The young man's possessions hold him back from following Jesus, and Jesus says it is harder for a rich man to enter the kingdom than for a camel to pass through a needle's eye. Wealth is not condemned in itself, but it is named as a rival for the heart, and the call to sell and give to the poor shows that following Jesus reorders what a person owns.

The young man asks what good thing he must do to obtain eternal life, and the disciples ask who then can be saved. Jesus answers that with man it is impossible but with God all things are possible (verse 26). Entrance into the kingdom is God's work, received as children receive, not achieved by keeping more rules.

The kingdom of heaven belongs to such as the children (verse 14), is hard for the rich to enter (verse 23), and reverses human rank: many who are first will be last (verse 30). It is present in Jesus' call to follow him and future in the renewal of all things.

Jesus speaks of ‘the renewal of all things’ (palingenesia, verse 28), when the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne and the twelve tribes are gathered. The age to come is a world made new, in which those who left houses and fields receive a hundredfold, not an escape from creation. The same chapter that appeals to God's design ‘from the beginning’ looks to its renewal at the end.

words.note: Apoluō, to release, send away, dismiss. It occurs about sixty-seven times in the New Testament, for releasing a prisoner (27:15), dismissing a crowd (14:15), and, as here, a husband's sending away of his wife, the ordinary Greek word for divorce. It appears four times in verses 3 to 9, and BDAG lists divorce as one sense of a verb whose basic idea is setting free. The Pharisees ask on what grounds a man may send his wife away; Jesus answers by asking what God has joined.

Porneia, sexual immorality. It occurs about twenty-five times in the New Testament and three times in Matthew (5:32, 15:19, 19:9). It is a broad word covering prostitution, fornication, adultery, and unlawful unions such as incest (1 Corinthians 5:1). Its breadth is why the exception is disputed: some take it as adultery, some as sexual sin in general, some as unfaithfulness during betrothal (compare 1:19), and some as marriage within the degrees of kinship forbidden in Leviticus 18, the reading Joseph Fitzmyer supported from the Dead Sea Scrolls. The word Matthew uses for adultery itself is a different one (moicheia).

Sklērokardia, hardness of heart, a compound of hard and heart. It occurs only three times in the New Testament: here, in the parallel Mark 10:5, and in Mark 16:14. The Greek Old Testament uses it in the call to circumcise the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16, Jeremiah 4:4). Jesus says Moses permitted divorce ‘because of’ it: the law set a limit on a broken practice rather than stating what God wanted, and the prophets hoped for the day God would replace hearts of stone with hearts of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26).

Eunouchos, eunuch. It occurs eight times in the New Testament, three times in verse 12 and five times of the Ethiopian official in Acts 8:27-39; the related verb eunouchizō, to make a eunuch, occurs only twice, both in verse 12. The Greek word meant a castrated man, often a court servant, and in the Greek Old Testament it renders the Hebrew saris, which could also mean a court official without implying castration. Jesus uses it literally for the first two kinds and figuratively for the third, those who forgo marriage for the kingdom.

Teleios, complete, whole, mature, perfect. It occurs about nineteen times in the New Testament and in the Gospels only in Matthew (5:48 twice, 19:21). In the Greek Old Testament it renders the Hebrew tamim, ‘whole, blameless’, used of Noah (Genesis 6:9) and required of Israel (Deuteronomy 18:13). Jesus does not grant the man a higher grade of holiness beyond ordinary obedience; he names the undivided heart the law always required, which for this man means giving up his possessions and following Jesus.

Kamēlos, camel. It occurs six times in the New Testament: John's clothing of camel's hair (3:4, Mark 1:6), this saying and its parallels (Mark 10:25, Luke 18:25), and the camel swallowed by teachers who strain out a gnat (23:24). Both sayings use the largest familiar animal for comic exaggeration. A few late manuscripts and some church writers read kamilos, ‘rope’, but that reading is secondary and the word itself is barely attested.

Palingenesia, renewal, rebirth, literally ‘becoming again’. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, here and in Titus 3:5, where it speaks of the washing of rebirth. Stoic philosophers used it for the renewal of the world after its periodic conflagration; Philo uses it of the renewed earth after the flood, with Noah's family as leaders of the new beginning (Life of Moses 2.65), and Josephus of the restoration of the Jewish homeland after the exile (Antiquities 11.66). Jesus uses it for the renewal of the world at the end of the age, when the Son of Man takes his throne.

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus speaking with an authority that stands behind Moses. The Pharisees ask what the law permits; he answers with what God did ‘from the beginning’, reading Deuteronomy by Genesis and placing his own ‘I tell you’ (verse 9) beside the Creator's intention. In Matthew the Messiah is the one who brings the law to its goal (5:17), and here he does so by recovering what the law's concession had obscured, while also shielding the one in the marriage who had no power to end it.

His answer to the young man points in the same direction. Matthew's wording, ‘Why do you ask Me about what is good? There is only One who is good’, turns the man from a good deed to the good God. Then Jesus asks for what only God has a right to ask: that the man leave everything and follow him. The one who is good is God, and the way to eternal life runs through following Jesus. Matthew does not state the conclusion in so many words, but he has already called Jesus Immanuel, God with us (1:23), and the scene makes loyalty to Jesus the one thing the man lacks.

The promise of verse 28 names Jesus as the Son of Man who will sit on his glorious throne. The title comes from Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man receives dominion and a kingdom, and Daniel's scene has thrones set for judgment (7:9) and a kingdom given to the saints (7:27). Matthew repeats the image at the last judgment (25:31). The twelve thrones make Jesus the one who restores the twelve tribes of Israel, the hope of Psalms of Solomon 17, and his followers share his reign. Yet the one who will sit on that throne is walking toward Jerusalem to be crucified, and the first to become last is Jesus himself, who, as Paul would say, became poor for the sake of others (2 Corinthians 8:9). The children he welcomes, the kingdom he says belongs to them, and the impossible salvation he says God can accomplish all point to the grace that the next chapter will set out in a parable and then in the ransom of 20:28.
interpretation:
Jesus' words on divorce have shaped Christian marriage law more than almost any other text, and the history has run in several channels. The Shepherd of Hermas (Mandate 4.1, second century) told a husband to separate from an unrepentant adulterous wife but not to remarry, so that she could return. Augustine argued that the bond remains while both spouses live (On the Good of Marriage, about 401; On Adulterous Marriages, about 419), and the Western church followed him. The Council of Trent (Session 24, 1563) affirmed that the bond is not dissolved even by adultery, while wording its canon so as not to condemn the Eastern churches, which by economy (oikonomia, pastoral dispensation) allow a second and, rarely, a third marriage with a penitential rite. Erasmus's annotations of 1519 argued that the innocent party might remarry; Luther's The Estate of Marriage (1522) allowed divorce for impotence, adultery, and refusal of marital relations; the Westminster Confession (1646, 24.5-6) permits divorce for adultery and for desertion that cannot be remedied. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (2382-2386) restates indissolubility and distinguishes the innocent victim of a civil divorce, and Pope Francis's apostolic exhortation Amoris Laetitia (2016), especially its eighth chapter and footnote 351, opened a debate among Catholics over the pastoral care of the divorced and civilly remarried that is not settled. In modern evangelical scholarship William Heth and Gordon Wenham (Jesus and Divorce, 1984) argued for separation without remarriage, a view Heth later abandoned; John Piper has read the exception as unfaithfulness during betrothal; David Instone-Brewer (Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible, 2002) read Jesus' answer as a rejection of the Hillelite ‘any cause’ divorce named in verse 3. The 1662 Book of Common Prayer puts verse 6 into the marriage service, where the priest declares that those whom God has joined no one may put asunder.

The eunuch saying has an unusual history. Eusebius reports that the young Origen took it literally and castrated himself (Church History 6.8.1-3). Origen's own Commentary on Matthew (15.1-5) argues strongly against a literal reading, and several modern historians doubt Eusebius's report or think it may reflect hostile rumor, though others accept it. The Council of Nicaea (325, canon 1) barred men who had castrated themselves from the clergy while allowing those castrated by illness or by others. The saying became a charter for consecrated celibacy. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I-II q.108 a.4) grounded the evangelical counsels in this chapter, chastity in verse 12 and poverty in verse 21, and the Catholic Church still grounds the celibacy of Latin-rite priests and of religious in the call to live ‘for the sake of the kingdom’ (Catechism 1579, 1618-1620). The Orthodox churches ordain married men as parish priests and choose bishops from the celibate monastic clergy. The Augsburg Confession (1530, article 23) cited verse 11 against compulsory clerical celibacy, since not all can receive this word, and Calvin (Institutes 4.13) rejected the idea that vows of celibacy or poverty confer a higher state. Jacques Dupont (Mariage et divorce dans l'évangile, 1959) and Quentin Quesnell (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1968) argued that in context the saying concerns those who, having separated from an unfaithful spouse, remain unmarried. More recently some scholars have read it as a place where Jesus welcomes people whose bodies or lives fall outside the ordinary path of marriage (J. David Hester, Journal for the Study of the New Testament, 2005), a reading others judge far from Matthew's purpose.

The young man's story founded a tradition. Clement of Alexandria's Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? (about 200) read it as a call to inner freedom from wealth rather than literal surrender. Athanasius tells how Antony of Egypt heard verse 21 read in church, sold his inherited land, and went into the desert (Life of Antony 2), and Francis of Assisi built his brotherhood on the same words. The medieval distinction between precepts binding all and counsels for those seeking perfection drew on verse 21; Calvin found it absurd that monks claimed a state of perfection from this passage (Institutes 4.13.13), and the Reformers read the command as a test that exposed the man's divided heart. Heinrich Hofmann's painting Christ and the Rich Young Ruler (1889), now in the Riverside Church in New York, became the best known image of the scene.
text:
English Bibles differ in several places in this chapter, mostly where the King James Version follows later manuscripts that harmonized Matthew with Mark and Luke.

Verse 4: the critical editions read ‘the Creator’ (ho ktisas), which the BSB follows; later manuscripts read ‘he who made’ (ho poiēsas), the KJV's ‘he which made them at the beginning’. Verse 9: the saying circulated in three forms. The text of most modern Bibles, found in Codex Sinaiticus among others, reads ‘except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman, commits adultery’. Codex Vaticanus and a few others give the exception in the wording of 5:32, ‘except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery’. Many manuscripts, including Vaticanus and the Byzantine majority, then add ‘and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery’, which the KJV prints (‘and whoso marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery’); editors judge it an addition from 5:32, and it is absent from Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae.

Verses 16 and 17: the earliest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, read ‘Teacher, what good thing’ and ‘Why do you ask Me about what is good? There is only One who is good’. Later manuscripts assimilated Matthew to Mark and Luke, reading ‘Good Teacher’ and ‘Why do you call Me good? There is none good but one, that is, God’, the form in the KJV. Bruce Metzger's Textual Commentary explains the later reading as a harmonization, and the earlier reading is the harder one. Verse 20: the KJV's ‘from my youth up’ comes from Mark and Luke and is absent from the earliest witnesses. Verse 24: a few late manuscripts read kamilon, ‘rope’, for kamēlon, ‘camel’.

Verse 29: manuscripts differ over the list of what is left. ‘Or wife’, from Luke 18:29, is absent from Vaticanus and some Western witnesses and is omitted by the critical editions (NA28, SBL); it is present in Sinaiticus and the majority of manuscripts, and the BSB and KJV include it. Vaticanus and a few others also read ‘many times as much’ (pollaplasiona), as in Luke 18:30, where most manuscripts have ‘a hundredfold’. In verse 28, English Bibles vary between ‘regeneration’ (KJV), ‘new world’ (ESV), and ‘renewal of all things’ (BSB, NIV) for the one Greek word palingenesia.

teach.big: Jesus measures marriage, childhood, wealth, and reward by God's purpose rather than by what is permitted or deserved: marriage is a union God makes, the kingdom belongs to those who can only receive it, and salvation, impossible for human beings, is possible for God.

outline.t: Jesus turns toward Jerusalem and the cross, and he still heals the crowds that follow him; everything he teaches on the road is spoken by one going to die.

Against a question about what a husband may do, Jesus asks what God has done: marriage is a one-flesh union he makes, the law's permission measured hard hearts, and the exception for sexual immorality does not turn divorce into a right.
Singleness for the kingdom is a gift and a calling, not a lesser life; not everyone can receive it, and those who can should.
The kingdom belongs to those with nothing to offer, and Jesus rebukes a church that keeps the smallest away from him.
A sincere and moral man lacks one thing because his possessions hold the place that belongs to following Jesus; the question is not what good deed remains but who is good.
Wealth makes entering the kingdom humanly impossible, and so does every form of self-reliance; salvation begins where human ability ends.
Nothing left for Jesus is lost, and his followers will share his reign when all things are renewed, but reward in the kingdom is never a ledger: many first will be last.

teach.pitfalls:
The divorce passage is often taught in one of two distorted ways. Some treat verse 9 as a rulebook that settles every case and ignore that Jesus was answering men who could dismiss a wife at will; others treat it as an ideal so distant that it asks nothing. Teach it in its setting and strength, and name honestly that Christian traditions read the exception clause differently (see the hard question below). Do not use it to shame people who have been divorced, many of whom did not choose it, and do not imply that it requires anyone to remain in danger.

The eunuch saying has been misused in opposite directions: as a command to literal self-harm, which the church rejected at Nicaea, or as a proof that celibacy is a higher grade of Christian life, which Jesus' own words (‘not everyone can accept this word’) do not support. It is also misused when it is ignored, leaving single people with the impression that the church has no place for them. Present marriage and singleness for the kingdom as two honored callings.

Verses 13 to 15 are often sentimentalized; ancient children stood for dependence and low status, not innocence. Verses 16 to 26 are softened by the needle-gate story or the rope reading, neither of which has ancient support, or confined to this one man, although Jesus generalizes the warning to his disciples. Verse 21 should not be taught as a two-tier ethic in which ordinary believers keep the commandments and the elite keep the counsels, nor as a universal command that every believer sell everything; it is a particular call that exposes a particular idol. Verse 29 has been used by prosperity teachers to promise a hundredfold return on gifts, but the hundredfold is given to those who have left houses and family, and it is joined to eternal life, not to a larger bank balance. Finally, avoid teaching verse 28 in a way that makes the disciples' reward a reason for pride; verse 30 immediately warns against it.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses hard on the divorced, the remarried, children of divorce, the single, and people in painful or dangerous marriages. Say plainly that Jesus spoke to men who held all the power to end a marriage, and that his words defended the one who could be sent away. Do not imply that every divorced person chose it; many were abandoned, betrayed, or endangered. Name the traditions fairly: the Catholic Church holds a valid sacramental marriage indissoluble while caring for the innocent spouse and examining claims of nullity, the Orthodox churches permit a second marriage in penitence, and most Protestant churches allow divorce and remarriage after adultery or desertion, many also after abuse. Let people seek their own church's counsel. Jesus' words never require anyone to remain where they or their children are in danger; separation for safety is not what this text condemns. Anyone facing abuse should seek safety first and help from their church and from qualified professionals, and this note is not legal advice. Single people, including those who did not choose to be single and those who cannot marry, should hear verse 12 as honor rather than as a verdict. People with scrupulous consciences may hear verse 21 as a demand they can never meet; remind them that the chapter's answer to ‘who then can be saved?’ is what God can do.

hard.q: Does Jesus allow divorce and remarriage, and what does ‘except for sexual immorality’ mean?
hard.a:
The objection is real and comes from several directions. Mark 10:11-12, Luke 16:18, and Paul, who cites the Lord's command (1 Corinthians 7:10-11), give Jesus' saying with no exception, while Matthew includes one here and in 5:32. Many historians, among them John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, volume 4, 2009), conclude that Jesus forbade divorce outright and that Matthew's exception shows the church adapting a demand it found too hard; skeptical readers take this as evidence that the evangelists edited Jesus when they needed to. Jewish readers object from the other side: the Torah itself regulates divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1-4), rabbinic tradition grieved divorce but never forbade it (b. Gittin 90b), and to call remarriage after a lawful divorce adultery seems to set Jesus against Moses and to trap people in marriages that have died. Critics of the church add that a strict reading has laid heavy burdens on betrayed and abused spouses, especially women.

Christians answer in different ways, and each view has serious defenders. The Catholic Church teaches that a valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power while both spouses live (Council of Trent, Session 24; Catechism 2382-2386); it permits separation, and it examines whether a true marriage existed in the first place. Some Catholic and other scholars, following Joseph Fitzmyer, read porneia here as marriage within forbidden degrees of kinship, so that the exception concerns unions that were never lawful. The Orthodox churches hold marriage to be lifelong in intent but permit a second and even a third marriage by economy, with a penitential rite. Most Protestant churches, following Erasmus and the Reformers, read the exception as permitting the innocent party to divorce and remarry after adultery, and add willful desertion from 1 Corinthians 7:15 (Westminster Confession 24.5-6); many now include abuse as desertion or covenant-breaking. Some evangelicals, including John Piper, read the exception as unfaithfulness during betrothal, as when Joseph resolved to divorce Mary (1:19), and allow no remarriage after a completed marriage; Heth and Wenham (1984) argued for separation without remarriage, as the early church largely held. David Instone-Brewer (2002) argues that verse 3's ‘for any reason’ names the Hillelite divorce Jesus rejected, and that Jesus did not thereby abolish the other biblical grounds of neglect and abuse (Exodus 21:10-11).

To the Jewish objection, Christian readers reply that Jesus does not deny that Moses wrote the law but reads it as a concession to hard hearts and appeals from Deuteronomy to Genesis, as the Damascus Document also did. No position should be taught as if faithful Christians had settled the question. What all share is Jesus' refusal to treat marriage as disposable and his protection of the one who could be sent away. This note is not legal advice; anyone facing separation or abuse should seek help from their church and from qualified professionals.

hard.q: Why does Matthew's Jesus say ‘Why do you ask Me about what is good?’ when Mark's Jesus says ‘Why do you call Me good?’ Did Matthew change his words, and does Jesus deny that he is good?
hard.a:
The objection has two parts. The first concerns the Gospels themselves. In Mark the man says ‘Good Teacher’ and Jesus replies ‘Why do you call Me good? No one is good except God alone’ (Mark 10:17-18), and Luke agrees (Luke 18:18-19). Matthew has the man ask about a good deed and Jesus reply about the good. Most scholars who hold that Matthew used Mark, including W. D. Davies and Dale Allison in the International Critical Commentary, conclude that Matthew reworded the exchange to avoid any suggestion that Jesus disclaimed goodness, and skeptical readers take this as proof that the evangelists altered Jesus' words to fit their theology. Later scribes felt the difference too and changed Matthew's text to match Mark, which is why the King James Version reads ‘Why callest thou me good?’ The second part concerns Christology. In the fourth century Arian theologians cited Mark's form to argue that Jesus distinguished himself from the one good God, and unitarian readers since have done the same; Jewish readers have also found in the saying a teacher pointing away from himself to God.

Responses begin with the texts. Ancient writers, including Greek and Roman biographers, commonly abridged and paraphrased speech while keeping its sense, and the evangelists clearly did so; the question is whether Matthew's form misrepresents the exchange. Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels 2.63) held that the man both addressed Jesus as good and asked what good thing he must do, and that the evangelists report Jesus' reply to different parts of the same exchange. Ned Stonehouse (Origins of the Synoptic Gospels, 1963) devoted a chapter to this passage and argued that Matthew's rewording is a faithful interpretation that brings out the point of the exchange, God's goodness as the measure of the law, and that recognizing it is compatible with a high view of Scripture. On the Christological question, Ambrose of Milan (On the Christian Faith 2.1) answered the Arians that Jesus was not denying his goodness but rebuking a man who called him a good teacher without believing him to be God, a reading many later interpreters share. In Matthew's form the saying points the man from a deed to the One who is good, and then Jesus calls the man to follow him, so that the goodness of God and the call of Jesus stand side by side. Christians who hold different views of how the Gospels were written agree that neither form denies Jesus' goodness; readers who do not share the church's confession will weigh the exchange differently, and the text itself leaves the man, and the reader, with the question of who Jesus is.

observe: How do the Pharisees describe what Moses did (verse 7), and how does Jesus describe it (verse 8)? Where does Jesus go to answer them?
What does the young man ask in verses 16 and 20, which commandments does Jesus list, and which one does Matthew alone include?
What two questions do the disciples and Peter ask in verses 25 and 27, and what does Jesus promise in answer?
interpret: Why does Jesus answer a question about what the law permits by going back to creation, and what does that suggest about how to read the law?
What do you think ‘this word’ in verse 11 refers to, and how does your answer change the meaning of the saying about eunuchs?
Why is it impossible for the rich to enter the kingdom ‘with man’, and what does verse 26 say about how anyone is saved?
apply: How does God's design ‘from the beginning’ shape the way you think about marriage, singleness, or your own relationships, and where do you need grace rather than a rule?
The young man asked what he still lacked. If you asked Jesus that question, what might he name?
Peter asked what the disciples would receive. In what ways do you keep accounts with God, and what would it look like to let go of them?
